newsitem.title: hong kong: Japan chopper, warships seen near HK protest ship.
newsitem.headline: Japan chopper, warships seen near HK protest ship.

text.p: A Japanese helicopter and four warships were sighted on Wednesday near a Hong Kong protest ship steaming towards disputed East China Sea islands that activists want to reclaim from Japan, radio and television reported.

The helicopter and four Japanese frigates circled the rusty tanker Kien Hwa 2 several times while it was some 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 km) from the islands, according to reporters on board quoted by Hong Kong radio and television stations.
"Protestors and journalists on board the Hong Kong protest ship reported the sighting at 9.00 a.m.," Asia Television said.

"They said they saw four armed warships carrying the Japanese flag circling the protest tanker at a distance of about 20 nautical miles," the station said. There was no information on whether the warships were still following the protest ship.
The ship, carrying 18 Hong Kong activists, 19 crew and 42 reporters, was due to arrive at the islands around 1430 GMT, Hong Kong government radio quoted correspondents on board as saying.

The activists have vowed to reclaim the islands, known in Chinese as the Diaoyus and in Japanese as the Senkakus, by removing the lighthouse and by raising the red flag of the People's Republic of China, government radio said.
Earlier, the group's spokesman in Hong Kong said they would not try to force their way on to the islands if they faced a strong Japanese military presence.
"Based on our principle of peaceful, rational, non-violent protest, and our members' safety, we will not make unnecessary sacrifices," Lew Mon-hung told reporters.

On Monday, five vessels carrying about 20 protesters from Taiwan and Hong Kong and up to 60 journalists tried to reach the islands to tear down the lighthouse. They were repulsed by 17 Japanese patrol ships backed by a helicopter.
Mainland China's long-time rival Taiwan said on Wednesday it would not protect the Hong Kong protest ship steaming toward the islands, but restated its resolve to defend its own claim.
The wife of activist David Chan, who is on board the tanker, appealed to the Japanese government not to use force.

"I appeal to the Japanese government not to do any barbaric act that will endanger the lives of those on board the ship," Hing Chan said. She also said China ought to show more concern for the protesters and protect the vessel.

The islands have been the focus of growing anti-Japanese protests by Chinese communities across East Asia and in North America since a Japanese rightist group built the lighthouse in July bolster Tokyo's sovereignty claim.
Japan has claimed sovereign rights to the islands and refused to acknowledge that the dispute is still open for discussion with China.
Japan's sovereignty claim dates to 1895, when Japan defeated China and seized Taiwan and other territories. China has claimed sovereignty over the islands for centuries.
